opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing it helped people see is that an agent doesn't have to live inside a chat window. For a long time, most people's mental model of AI was: you open an app, type a question, get an answer, close the app. It's a very passive, turn-by-turn relationship.

What something like Open Cloud showed is that you can give a model a persistent environment. It has a computer, it has your files, it has your messaging apps, it can run things in the background, and it can come back to you when something's done. Suddenly it feels less like a tool you query and more like a colleague or an assistant who's always on. That shift is psychological as much as technical, because the underlying models were already fairly capable. What was missing was the scaffolding and the permission to let them actually act.

The second thing is that it came from the open community, not from a big lab's product team. That told people the bottleneck isn't only model capability. A lot of the value is in how you wire the model into real workflows, and individual developers can explore that space very quickly. People started realizing that the "last mile," meaning integration, memory, tool access, and long-running tasks, is where a lot of the experienced intelligence comes from.

And honestly, it also made people confront the risks more concretely. Once an agent can read your email and execute commands, questions about security, trust, and what you're willing to delegate stop being abstract. So in a way it opened up the possibility space and made people take it seriously at the same time.

r001.rationale: The response mentions background activity and long-running tasks, but does not say Open Cloud demonstrated very long-horizon work orchestrated across multiple AI models.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest thing OpenClaw did was make a lot of people realize that the bottleneck for agents is no longer the model. For the past couple of years, if you asked why agents weren't useful, the honest answer was usually "the model isn't good enough yet." OpenClaw showed that with the models we already have, if you just give the agent the right environment — your messages, your files, your calendar, your browser, a persistent memory, and the ability to run all the time rather than only when you open a chat window — suddenly a lot of long-tail things become possible. Nobody trained a new model for that. It was a harness problem, not an intelligence problem.

The second thing is about who gets to define what an agent is. Before, the mental model was that an agent is a product shipped by a lab or a big company, and you use it inside their interface. OpenClaw flipped that. It's your agent, running on your machine, with your context, and you can wire it to whatever you want. The community ended up exploring a huge design space very fast — skills, memory structures, how to handle long-running tasks, how to make it proactive instead of reactive. Many of those ideas are things a lab would take months to decide to try, and here you had thousands of people trying them in parallel. That's a kind of research too, just not in the form of papers.

And honestly, the third thing is a bit uncomfortable for people like me who come from the benchmark side. OpenClaw became popular without a benchmark telling anyone it was good. People just used it and felt the value. That tells you our evaluations are measuring something, but they're missing a lot of what actually matters when an agent lives in your life over weeks — memory, continuity, trust, knowing when to interrupt you. I've been saying that the second half of AI is about redefining problems and evaluation rather than just training better models, and OpenClaw is a very concrete example of that. It showed a possibility, and now the question is how we study it seriously.

r001.rationale: The response describes persistent context and agents running continuously, but it does not say OpenClaw demonstrated very long-horizon work by orchestrating multiple AI models.

astra-6.text: I think Open Cloud helped people recognize that AI could be more than something you chat with. It could actually do things for you—use tools, carry out a task, and help move work forward. That makes a different kind of interaction imaginable: instead of guiding the model through every step, you give it a goal and let it handle more of the process. It doesn’t mean that everything is reliable yet, but it makes that possibility much more concrete.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI using tools and handling more of a task, but it does not identify very long-horizon work or orchestration of multiple AI models.

sol-6.1.text: I think Open Cloud helped people recognize the possibility that an AI could do more than answer questions—it could actually help you get things done. You give it a goal, and it uses tools, interacts with software, and takes a sequence of actions toward that goal. That changes how you imagine the relationship between people and AI: from something you consult to something you can delegate work to. It doesn’t mean the technology is already reliable enough for every task, but it makes that possibility much more tangible.

r001.rationale: The response describes goal-directed tool use and sequences of actions, but does not say Open Cloud can orchestrate multiple AI models or carry out very long-horizon work.
